title: Axe to knife progression
subtitle: How to move between the carving axe and the sloyd knife without losing your line
excerpt: The two-tool progression, axe for bulk removal, knife for detail, is the foundation of all green-wood carving. Getting the transition right means knowing when the axe has done its job, how to read the axe surface before picking up the knife, and how to keep control of form through the shift. Beginners who skip the axe work too hard with the knife; those who skip the knife lose control of the final shape.
sourceNotes: Cassell's Cyclopaedia of Mechanics vol. III (1885) for the axe-to-knife principle in green woodwork; Newey & Drage Practical Carpentry for the surface reading technique.

glossaryTerms.definition: Freshly felled or recently riven wood. The axe removes large amounts quickly; the knife refines the surface.
A short section of split or round timber, the starting point for most green-woodwork carving.

content.text: The carving axe removes ten times the material of the sloyd knife with each cut; the knife takes a surface the axe cannot produce. Used together in sequence they make any spoon, kuksa, or
green-woodwork
piece far faster than either alone. The key is knowing where the boundary is. There is a specific moment when the axe hands off to the knife, and reading that moment is what this technique is about.
When to use this technique
Whenever a green-woodwork project starts from a raw
billet
: spoons, kuksa blanks, mallets, pegs, or any form that requires moving from round log section to final shape. Not needed if working directly from a drawknife or a shaving horse.
What the axe does

The carving axe is used to establish the main planes of the form. On a spoon blank: the axe removes the log-round section to produce a flat back and defines the profile. On a kuksa: the axe shapes the handle and rounds the cup exterior. The axe leaves a surface that is close to the final form but with visible facets, flat planes left by each axe cut.
When the axe is done

The axe is done when the blank is within 5, 7 mm of the final form on all surfaces. The test: sight along the blank and compare the profile to the intended shape. If any plane is more than 5 mm proud of the final surface, the axe can take another pass. If all surfaces are within 5 mm, the axe has done its job. Starting the knife before this point means slow, tiring knife work across large areas; taking the axe past this point means cutting through the final form.
Reading the axe surface before picking up the knife

Before picking up the knife, run a thumb over the axe surface. A correctly prepared blank has facets, flat surfaces meeting at slight angles. Each facet tells the knife where one axe cut stopped. The knife's job is to blend these facets into a smooth surface. Identify the three or four large facets on the blank; these are the areas the knife will work first, to bring the whole surface to an even distance from the final form before any detail work begins.
The knife stage
Use
push cuts

to blend the facets: hold the blank steady with one hand and push the knife along the grain with the other, taking a consistent shaving that bridges across each facet ridge. Work all the facets evenly, do not refine one area completely before moving on; keep the whole surface advancing together toward the final form. Only in the last stage does detailed knife work define the final edge curves, the handle profile, or the spoon neck.
Common errors
Picking up the knife too early: the blank is still at log-section width on one side, so knife work on the narrow parts is out of proportion with the fat parts.
Leaving the axe too late: the axe cuts through the final form and leaves a hollow that cannot be recovered.
Refining one area first: the blank ends up with one refined section and the rest still at axe-finish. These cannot be blended without removing the refined part. Work all surfaces together.

attrs.symptom: The knife cuts leave a raised ridge between two facets instead of blending them
attrs.cause: The cut starts on the high facet and stops at the ridge rather than bridging across both facets
attrs.fix: Start the cut on the high facet and continue it 2, 3 cm past the ridge into the lower facet, taking a shaving that spans the junction. A long cut that crosses the ridge blends it; a short cut that stops at the ridge leaves a step.
